title: Penguin Body Mass Analysis
text:
In this post, we explore how body mass differs across three penguin species: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo.
The dataset comes from the Palmer Penguins project
The Palmer Penguins dataset is distributed under the CC0 license.

title: Penguin Body Mass Analysis
text:
Chunk 1: Load Data
First, we load the R packages required for our analysis.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data("penguins")

head(penguins)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA          NA
5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>


The dataset contains measurements such as body mass, bill length, flipper length, species, and island.

title: Penguin Body Mass Analysis
text:
Chunk 2: Clean data
Before calculating summary statistics, we remove observations with missing species or body mass values.

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  filter(
    !is.na(species),
    !is.na(body_mass_g)
  )

cat("Original observations:", nrow(penguins), "\n")

Original observations: 344 

cat("Clean observations:", nrow(penguins_clean), "\n")

Clean observations: 342 


Removing missing values ensures that our body mass calculations use observations with valid measurements.

title: Penguin Body Mass Analysis
text:
Chunk 3: Calculate statistics
Next, we group the observations by species and calculate the number of penguins, mean body mass, and standard deviation of body mass.

penguin_summary <- penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass_g),
    sd_body_mass = sd(body_mass_g),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

penguin_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species   count mean_body_mass sd_body_mass
  <fct>     <int>          <dbl>        <dbl>
1 Adelie      151          3701.         459.
2 Chinstrap    68          3733.         384.
3 Gentoo      123          5076.         504.


These summary statistics allow us to compare the typical body mass and variability across the three species.

title: Penguin Body Mass Analysis
text:
Chunk 4: Visualization
We use a boxplot to compare the distribution of body mass across penguin species.

ggplot(
  penguins_clean,
  aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Penguin Body Mass by Species",
    x = "Penguin Species",
    y = "Body Mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Figure 1: Distribution of body mass across three penguin species.





The boxplot shows differences in the body mass distributions across species.
In conclusion, our analysis shows that Gentoo penguins have a higher average body mass than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.

title: Iris Petal Length Analysis
text: In this post, we investigate how petal length differs across three Iris species: Setosa, Versicolor, and Virginica. The dataset is available through scikit-learn’s Iris dataset.

title: Iris Petal Length Analysis
text:
Chunk 1: Load data
First, we import the Python libraries required for our analysis.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)

iris_df = iris.frame.copy()

iris_df["species"] = iris_df["target"].map(
    dict(enumerate(iris.target_names))
)

title: Iris Petal Length Analysis
text:
Chunk 2: Clean data
Before analyzing petal length, we check for missing values and remove observations with missing petal length or species information.

missing_values = iris_df.isna().sum()

print("Missing values:")
print(missing_values)

iris_clean = iris_df.dropna(
    subset=["petal length (cm)", "species"]
).copy()

print("Original observations:", len(iris_df))
print("Clean observations:", len(iris_clean))

Checking for missing values helps us ensure that the summary statistics are based on valid observations.

title: Iris Petal Length Analysis
text:
Chunk 3: Calculate statistics
Next, we group the observations by species and calculate the mean and standard deviation of petal length.

iris_summary = (
    iris_clean
    .groupby("species")["petal length (cm)"]
    .agg(
        count="count",
        mean_petal_length="mean",
        sd_petal_length="std"
    )
    .reset_index()
)

title: Iris Petal Length Analysis
text:
Chunk 4: Visualization
We use a boxplot to compare the distribution of petal length across the three species.

species_names = [
    "setosa",
    "versicolor",
    "virginica"
]

petal_lengths = [
    iris_clean.loc[
        iris_clean["species"] == species,
        "petal length (cm)"
    ]
    for species in species_names
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

ax.boxplot(
    petal_lengths,
    tick_labels=species_names
)

ax.set_title("Iris Petal Length by Species")
ax.set_xlabel("Iris Species")
ax.set_ylabel("Petal Length (cm)")

plt.show()







Figure 1: Distribution of petal length across three Iris species.





The boxplot illustrates differences in the distribution of petal length across species. We can compare the median, spread, and potential outliers for each species.
In conclusion, our analysis shows that Iris setosa has the shortest average petal length, while Iris virginica has the longest average petal length among the three species.
